claims.text: A machine-learning interatomic potential can serve as an efficient surrogate for explicit AIMD in multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
The surrogate can be used for free-energy integration across both solid and liquid states near and above melting.
Moment tensor potentials can reproduce underlying DFT energies and forces for a multicomponent MoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloy with a favorable balance of accuracy and computational cost.
Training on comprehensive high-temperature ab initio data will allow the ML potential to interpolate the relevant ab initio potential-energy surface.
The ML potential will encode vibrational entropy accurately during free-energy evaluation.
The ML potential will encode high-temperature anharmonicity accurately during free-energy evaluation.
The ML potential will encode electron–vibration coupling accurately during free-energy evaluation.
Vibrational entropy is a relevant and composition-dependent contribution to high-entropy-alloy thermodynamics.
Coupling the ML potential to enhanced free-energy sampling will capture all relevant vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration thermodynamic contributions.
The resulting phase free energies will closely mirror those from explicit AIMD.
The proposed method will reduce computational cost by one to two orders of magnitude relative to explicit AIMD.
Phase free energies, melting temperatures, and heat capacities will remain within 5% of explicit-AIMD results.
The method will provide greater throughput than TOR-TILD for complex multicomponent systems.
ML-potential training can span elemental, binary, ternary, and quaternary compositional subsets.
The method is applicable only within temperature and composition regimes robustly represented in the training data.
Extrapolation to unsampled compositions, temperatures, or extreme anharmonic regimes may reduce fidelity.
Explicit AIMD free-energy calculations and TOR-TILD become prohibitively expensive or slow for multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
The melting temperature can be obtained from equality of the solid and liquid phase free energies.
A deviation greater than 5% from explicit AIMD or a speedup below tenfold relative to AIMD would falsify the hypothesis.
